title: Metzora: coming back in (Leviticus 14:8–9)
hookLine: washed and renewed, the person returns to the camp

cards: Coming back is its own kind of hard. The first day at work after a long illness. A family dinner after a year of not speaking.
Stepping out of prison, or rehab, or a hospital, into a world that kept going without you. Where do you sit? Leviticus has followed a person outside the camp for two chapters now.
The priest came out. The bird flew free. And now the Torah does something careful: it doesn't just open the gate.
It walks them back in, step by step.

teach.h: VE-TAHER: AND HE SHALL BE CLEAN.
teach.b: It starts with washing. The person washes their clothes, shaves their hair, and bathes in water. Twice in two verses the Hebrew says ve-taher, and he shall be clean.
Then they come into the camp, but not all at once.

Even inside, they stay outside their own tent for seven more days. On the seventh day they shave again, head, beard and eyebrows, wash again, bathe again. The Torah doesn't pretend re-entry is a single moment.

teach.h: EAR, THUMB, TOE, LIKE A PRIEST.
teach.b: Back in Tzav, sixteen days ago on this path, when the priests were ordained, blood was placed on the right ear, the right thumb, the right big toe. Listen, do, walk.
Now the same three places are touched on the person who has just come back: blood, and then oil, on ear, thumb and toe. The one who was outside the camp is marked the way the priests were marked.
Some readers hear it this way: not as damaged goods, but as someone beginning again. And the way back has a name.

Jewish tradition calls returning teshuvah, and insists the door is never fully shut. Maimonides writes that a person who returns should not think they are far from the virtue of the righteous. Hair grows back.
There is a way back, and it has steps.

how: Jewish tradition teaches teshuvah, return, as always possible; communities welcome people back after illness or estrangement, and someone recovered from serious illness may say Birkat Hagomel, a blessing of thanks, at the Torah reading.

o: the afflicted one, now walked back home
the seven days spent outside one's own tent
a priest's ordination on ear, thumb and toe

games.q: what's inside the return — tap the pairs.

s: the person came straight home the day they were declared clean
they came into the camp but stayed outside their tent for seven more days.
on the seventh day, the returning person shaved head, beard and eyebrows
then washed and bathed again, before the eighth day.
Maimonides says one who returns stays far from the righteous
he says they should not think themselves far from the virtue of the righteous.

games.q: you've washed, shaved and bathed, and you're allowed back into the camp. what does the Torah have you do next?
o: go straight home to your tent.
stay outside your tent seven more days.
go to the sanctuary to serve.
games.why: seven more days outside your tent, then wash again, and on the eighth day the offerings. coming back takes a week.

practice: Think of someone trying to come back in after being away, by illness, a mistake or a falling-out: a coworker back from leave, a relative who messed up, a friend who went quiet.
Picture their first awkward moment back, and yourself making it easier with a greeting, a saved seat, a normal question. Not a speech; a step.

wordCard.voice: Metzora. The portion that walks the afflicted person back into the camp, step by step, and marks them on ear, thumb and toe like a priest.

orig.note: Hebrew: "and he shall be clean": the word repeated through the return in Leviticus 14:8–9.

carryVoice: Your line: there is a way back. The door is never fully shut. Rest well.

sources.ref: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Repentance 7:4
